activities.anchor: ignoring constant factors and small-input noise
activities.caption: bet before you read on — what separates the survivor from the forever-runner
activities.name: gofnPredict

config.q: Both algorithms answer correctly and feel instant on a 1,000-item input. What separates them at a million items?
choices: How their cost grows as the input gets larger
The speed of the processor each runs on
How recently the code was written
The programming language each is written in
config.why: Big-O names the growth curve; at scale that growth — not hidden multipliers, hardware or taste — picks the survivor and the forever-runner.

activities.anchor: Doubling the data adds exactly one step.
activities.caption: which curve pays just one extra unit when the input doubles?
activities.name: gofnTrace

config.prompt: When the input doubles, this curve rises by a single extra unit — which is it?
config.why: Logarithmic: each pass discards half of what remains, so a billion sorted items need about 30 — binary search's signature.

activities.caption: call the bill for one quadratic pass
activities.name: gofnQuadEst

config.prompt: A quadratic routine runs once over 100,000 inputs — roughly how many steps does it cost?
config.why: n² = 10¹⁰ — ten billion. At 100 ns per comparison, a single pass costs about a quarter of an hour.
config.context: At 1,000 inputs the same routine cost a million steps — the input grew 100×, the bill 10,000×.

activities.anchor: Zoom into the left edge of the plot above and you can see the curves tangle
activities.caption: true or false — what Big-O does and does not promise
activities.name: gofnBigOJudge

statements.s: Big-O predicts a program's running time in seconds.
statements.why: It names a growth rate — a shape, never a stopwatch reading.

statements.s: On lists of a dozen items, O(n²) insertion sort can genuinely finish before merge sort.
statements.why: Hidden multipliers dominate at small sizes — which is exactly why real libraries hand small sublists to insertion sort.

statements.s: Once two algorithms differ in Big-O, the better one is guaranteed to win on every input size.
statements.why: The guarantee is asymptotic only; for tiny inputs the 'worse' algorithm can win.

statements.s: Engineers profile before optimising because measurement and analysis are companions, not rivals.
statements.why: Small-size behaviour can mislead — look before you leap.

activities.caption: two sorters, opposite bargains — drag the divider
activities.name: gofnSpaceCompare

config.prompt: Two in-family sorters, opposite bargains — drag the divider:

before.label: merge sort
before.text: O(n log n) speed, paid for with O(n) extra space — room for a second array during the merge.

after.label: heapsort
after.text: Sorts in place with O(1) extra memory — the same asymptotics, a different bargain.

config.why: The two budgets trade constantly; 'fewer bytes moved' is often the real reason an algorithm wins.

activities.anchor: Complexity is not an accident; it is designed in.
activities.caption: the standard method, start to finish
activities.name: gofnDesignOrder

config.prompt: Build an algorithm the standard way — put the stages in order:
items: Abstraction: discard details irrelevant to the problem — keep road connections and journey times, forget scenery and tarmac.
Decomposition: break the problem into sub-problems until each is directly codeable.
Write the solution in structured English, pseudocode or a flowchart — every decision forced, nothing implementation-bound.
Only then write the code, carrying those decisions across.
config.why: Abstraction → decomposition → design → code: skipping ahead is how trouble gets baked in.

activities.caption: find the faulty verdict — count the loops
activities.name: gofnLoopsSpot

config.prompt: One of these loop-counting verdicts is wrong — click it:
lines: One loop over n items: O(n).
A loop inside a loop over the same n: usually O(n²).
A loop that halves the problem each pass: O(log n).
An O(n) pass followed by an O(n log n) sort: O(n² log n).
config.correction: Costs in sequence add — O(n) followed by O(n log n) is O(n log n); only nesting multiplies.
config.why: Count the loops: nesting multiplies, sequence adds — that is the whole heuristic.

activities.anchor: The binary search's sorted-data condition is worth pausing on, because it is the classic exam trap.
activities.caption: a million-record lookup — design the access
activities.name: gofnPrecondBranch

config.root: A million-record lookup list, queried thousands of times a day. Design the access.

start.text: The list arrives jumbled. First move?

choices.label: Sort once (O(n log n)), then halve every lookup
choices.feedback: The one-time sort buys logarithmic lookups forever after — which is why databases fight so hard to stay indexed.

choices.label: Skip the sort; scan every query end to end
choices.feedback: O(n) each time and works on any order — fine for a few queries, ruinous at thousands a day.

indexed.text: Sorted and quick. A colleague hands you tomorrow's data — jumbled again.

choices.label: Re-sort before searching
choices.feedback: The guarantee is only as good as its precondition — check what the method assumes, every time.

choices.label: Search directly; it usually works
choices.feedback: Run the logarithmic method on jumbled data and it confidently returns wrong answers.

linear.text: Simple, correct — and slow at scale.

choices.label: Switch to sort-once-then-halve as volume grows
choices.feedback: Amortise the one-time sort across millions of lookups and the trade is a landslide.

choices.label: Stay linear forever
choices.feedback: The bill grows with the data — about 500,000 comparisons per lookup on a million records.

broken.text: Confident, quick, and wrong: the algorithm's guarantee is only as good as its precondition.

discipline.text: In order once, halved forever after — the precondition is part of the method.

slow.text: O(n) to the end — sometimes the honest choice, but know the bill.

config.why: Sorting costs n log n once and every lookup after is logarithmic — but only on data in order; before using any standard method, check what it assumes.
